name: Hungarian Agricultural Museum and Library
description: Vajdahunyad Castle in City Park is a Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque ensemble designed by Ignác Alpár and built for the 1896 Millennium celebrations. The museum was founded in the same year and holds the national collection on agriculture, hunting, fishing and related food-industry material.

children.text: The Hungarian Agricultural Museum occupies the Baroque wing of Vajdahunyad Castle in City Park. The castle was designed by Ignác Alpár and built in 1896 for the Millennium celebrations marking a thousand years since the Hungarian conquest. It was first a set of copies of historical buildings, made mainly of wood and cardboard, and its main façade copies Hunyad Castle in Vajdahunyad, today Hunedoara in Romania, which gave it its name.

The museum itself was founded in 1896. According to Hungarian Wikipedia, the founding decree was signed on 20 June 1896 by the agriculture minister Ignác Darányi, and the museum opened in the castle on 12 September 1897 under its first director, Árpád Balás. The temporary structure was not built to last. It was closed in July 1899 and demolished, and the museum moved to a rented house on Kerepesi út until the castle was rebuilt.

The rebuilding in brick and stone was approved in 1900 and followed Alpár's plans, with the Gothic and Renaissance-Baroque wings finished in 1904 and the Romanesque section in 1908. The museum moved back in 1904, and Franz Joseph I reopened it on 9 June 1907. English Wikipedia gives 1907 for the opening of the exhibition, so the dates in the sources differ slightly. The castle was declared a monument in 1991.

Hungarian Wikipedia reports that the museum has 39 collections and that in 2016 it was estimated to hold more than 400,000 objects. Notable holdings include the first steam locomotive to arrive in Hungary in 1852, a trophy collection and a collection of wheat varieties. In 2015 the Gate Tower and the Apostles' Tower were opened to visitors, and the same year original plans by Alpár were found in a walled-up room.

The courtyard holds Miklós Ligeti's statue of Anonymus, the unknown chronicler at the court of King Béla III, and the Ják Chapel stands in the castle grounds but is not run by the museum. The museum's library has been merged with the national agricultural library, and its holdings in the castle were moved to Attila út in 2019 and 2020.
Good to know
The castle is in City Park, so it combines easily with a walk around the lake and the other buildings of the park.
Relocation of the museum has been discussed in recent years; check the official site for the current status, opening times and tickets before you go.
The statue of Anonymus stands in the castle courtyard, and the Ják Chapel is in the castle grounds.
Sources
Hungarian Wikipedia: Magyar Mezőgazdasági Múzeum
Wikipedia: Vajdahunyad Castle

heroImage.alt: The ornate Baroque wing of Vajdahunyad Castle that houses the Hungarian Agricultural Museum

historyIntro: The Agricultural Museum is housed in Vajdahunyad Castle, a building born from the celebrations of Hungary's millennium in 1896.

historySections.heading: A romantic castle made for a public exhibition

children.text: The story begins with the 1896 celebrations marking a thousand years of Hungarian statehood. Vajdahunyad Castle gathered architectural references from different periods to present the country's past in a single picturesque setting.

historySections.heading: Farming history in the city park

children.text: The Agricultural Museum and Library use the castle to explore Hungary's agricultural heritage, tools, crops and rural life. The contrast between romantic architecture and practical subjects is part of what makes the visit distinctive.

name: Hungarian Natural History Museum
description: Hungary's national natural history museum grew out of collections given to the National Museum in the early nineteenth century. Its exhibition building stands in the Ludovika complex in Pest's eighth district, and its collections cover anthropology, zoology, minerals and fossils.

children.text: The Hungarian Natural History Museum, Magyar Természettudományi Múzeum, grew out of the Hungarian National Museum. In 1802 Count Ferenc Széchényi gave his library and coin collection to the nation, and his wife Julianna Festetics later donated a mineral collection that became the root of the natural science collections. Archduke Rainer gave the first palaeontological collection in 1811, and in 1818 the botanical department began with the plant collection of Pál Kitaibel.

Separate departments for zoology, botany and mineralogy were created within the National Museum in 1870. The zoological department moved to a building at Baross utca 13 in 1928, partly because of the 1927 International Zoological Congress in Budapest, and a partly independent natural history museum was set up in 1933. An anthropology department was created soon after 1945, and the museum became independent in 1949.

The 1956 revolution caused heavy losses. The National Museum building was hit on 24 October, destroying parts of the Africa exhibition and mineral and palaeontological material, and on 5 November an incendiary bomb struck the Baross utca building, destroying tens of thousands of specimens and about a hundred thousand books and offprints.

In 1994 the government decided to place the museum in the Ludovika Academy complex, a historic site originally built as a military academy. Collections began moving in from 1995, and the exhibition building opened in 1996. The museum's own history page describes the exhibition building as the rebuilt Ludovika riding hall, the former Alfa cinema building that burned down in 1992. Other Hungarian sources add that the Alfa cinema opened there in 1958 and closed in 1990, and that a fire in May 1992 destroyed the roof structure. The Ludovika site now houses mineralogy, geology and palaeontology, anthropology, parts of zoology and the library.

The anthropology collection is described as one of the ten largest in Europe. Since 1 July 2024 the museum has been a branch institution of the Hungarian National Museum Public Collection Centre. Moving the museum out of Ludovika has been discussed since 2010 without a move taking place, so its exhibitions are best checked before a visit.
Good to know
The exhibition site is at Ludovika tér 2 to 6 in the eighth district; the nearest metro stops on line M3 are Semmelweis Klinikák and Nagyvárad tér.
Check the official site for current exhibitions, opening times and tickets, since the museum's future location has been under discussion.
The botanical collection is housed in an Art Nouveau palace on Könyves Kálmán körút that a source says is not open to visitors.

heroImage.alt: The curved modern entrance pavilion of the Hungarian Natural History Museum

historyIntro: Budapest's Natural History Museum opens a window into the country's scientific collecting tradition and the diversity of life and geology.

children.text: The museum's origins lie in the historic study and preservation of the natural world. Over generations, scientists assembled animal, plant, mineral and fossil collections that support both public understanding and research.

Exhibitions use specimens and explanations to show how habitats, species and geological landscapes change. Scientific collections hold evidence far older than Budapest itself and remind visitors that the region's natural history is part of a much larger world.

name: Franz Liszt Memorial Museum and Research Centre
description: On the first floor of the Old Academy of Music on Vörösmarty utca, the museum preserves the apartment where Franz Liszt stayed whenever he was in Budapest from 1881 until his death in 1886. His pianos, desk, library and furniture are displayed in the rooms where he lived.

children.text: The Liszt Ferenc Memorial Museum and Research Centre is in the Old Academy of Music at Vörösmarty utca 35, just off Andrássy út. It opened in September 1986 and occupies the building in which the Academy of Music taught from 1879 to mid-1907, after its first four years in a building on Hal tér. The Academy had been founded with Liszt as its founding president and a professor, and he took no salary for his teaching.

Liszt was given a service apartment on the first floor and lived there, whenever he stayed in Budapest, from January 1881 until his death in 1886. The apartment is now the memorial museum, furnished with his instruments, furniture, library and personal belongings. A visitor article notes that the rooms look little changed and that the furniture in the two larger rooms stands where it did in his time.

Look for the walnut writing desk in the corner of the study-bedroom, made for him by his friend the piano maker Ludwig Bösendorfer, with a pull-out three-octave keyboard in place of the middle drawer, which Liszt could use to try out passages. The core collection is Liszt's donation to the Academy and includes a Bösendorfer and two Chickering pianos, a Mason & Hamlin cabinet organ, a combined piano and organ by Erard and Alexandre, and a piano-harmonica by Bachmann. His Budapest library of books and scores is also here.

After the Academy moved to its new palace on Liszt Ferenc tér on 12 May 1907, the building was used by a music school, a coffee shop, associations and a foreign trade company. The Ministry of Culture and Education bought it in 1980 and gave it to the Academy of Music. A first Liszt memorial room had opened in the new Academy building in 1925, and the research centre was founded together with the museum in 1986.

Some key exhibits are on loan from the Hungarian National Museum, which Liszt himself had given important relics from his career. Documents and memorabilia from relatives and pupils, among them Eduard Liszt, Jenő Hubay and István Thomán, have also been added over the decades, together with later purchases and bequests.
Good to know
The museum is at Vörösmarty utca 35, in front of the Vörösmarty utca stop of the Millennium Underground on Andrássy út.
The concert hall next to the apartment hosts concerts, so check the official site for the current programme, opening times and tickets.
The former dining room and ground-floor foyer are used for temporary exhibitions, so what you see may vary.

heroImage.alt: The yellow and grey facade of the Old Music Academy building, home of the Franz Liszt Memorial Museum

historyIntro: The Franz Liszt Memorial Museum keeps the pianist and composer's life close to the city where he helped establish a lasting musical institution.

children.text: Franz Liszt was central to the establishment of the academy of music that carries his name. His connections with Budapest made the city an important centre for his later work, teaching and musical advocacy.

The memorial museum is linked to the Liszt Academy and its research centre. Its permanent exhibition fills the entrance room, Liszt's study-bedroom and the drawing room, while the former dining room and the ground-floor foyer host temporary Liszt exhibitions.

name: Ferenc Hopp Museum of Asiatic Arts
description: A museum of Asian art in the villa on Andrássy út where the optician and collector Ferenc Hopp lived. It grew from his bequest to the state and now holds Chinese, Japanese, Indian, Tibetan and other collections, with a garden that still contains the statues and pagodas he installed.

children.text: The Ferenc Hopp Museum of Asiatic Arts is at Andrássy út 103, in the villa and garden that its founder left to the state. Ferenc Hopp, an optician and photographer who took over the Calderoni optical firm in 1864, was born in Fulnek in Moravia in 1833 and died in Budapest on 9 September 1919.

Hopp made five journeys around the world, with a focus on East Asia, especially China and Japan, and he lectured on his travels to the Hungarian Geographical Society. Hungarian Wikipedia says he bought about 1,200 Chinese objects between 1883 and 1914 and that his Japanese collection numbered nearly 2,000 items at his death. His collection also drew on Africa, America and Australia, but East Asian art was the standout.

In 1919 he left the villa, the garden and several thousand objects to the state. Sources give the number as about 4,000 to more than 4,500 items. His will required that the building be used as an East Asian art museum and that the museum always bear his name. It opened in 1923, and its collection has grown through gifts, purchases and transfers from other museums, including the Zichy North Asian collections and the Indian collection of Imre Schwaiger.

The collection now covers China, Japan, India, Southeast Asia, Nepal, Tibet, Mongolia, Korea and the Middle East. Japanese medieval art and Chinese bronzes and porcelain are especially significant. Hungarian Wikipedia gives about 23,000 objects in 2006, while a 2021 article says about 30,000, so the figure depends on the source. After 1945 the museum also received state gifts from Vietnam, China and North Korea.

The villa garden still holds the Asian statues, pagodas and memorial columns that Hopp erected. The museum is part of the Budapest World Heritage site and is a specialist museum of the Museum of Fine Arts.
Good to know
The museum is on Andrássy út at number 103, a stretch of the avenue with several other museums and villas near the City Park end.
Temporary exhibitions focus on individual Asian countries and peoples; check the official site for what is on, plus opening times and tickets.
Allow a few minutes to walk around the garden, which is part of what Hopp left to the state.

heroImage.alt: The villa of the Ferenc Hopp Museum of Asiatic Arts behind its iron fence and trees

historyIntro: The museum exists because of one man's will. Ferenc Hopp, a Budapest optician who travelled widely in Asia, left his villa, garden and collection to the state in 1919 on condition that they become a museum bearing his name.

children.text: Ferenc Hopp was born in Fulnek in Moravia on 28 April 1833. Hungarian Wikipedia says he began as an optician's apprentice at the age of thirteen under István Calderoni, was sent to Vienna in 1853 and then to New York, returned in 1861 and took over the firm in 1864 while keeping its name. The firm made optical instruments and cameras and introduced the manufacture of school teaching aids to Hungary. Once he could afford to travel, he made five journeys around the world; sources date them slightly differently, but all place them between the early 1880s and the 1910s. East Asia, above all China and Japan, drew him most. Hungarian Wikipedia says he bought about 1,200 Chinese objects between 1883 and 1914, and his Japanese collection reached nearly 2,000 items by his death.

Hopp died in Budapest on 9 September 1919. In his will he left his villa and garden at Andrássy út 103 and his collection to the Hungarian state. Sources give the size of the collection as about 4,000 to more than 4,500 objects. He had first thought of dividing the collection among the Museum of Fine Arts, the Museum of Applied Arts and the Ethnographic Museum, but he decided instead on a single museum. His will required that the villa be used as an East Asian art museum and that the museum should always carry his name. It also required that other state-owned Eastern collections be added to his own.

The Ferenc Hopp Museum of Asiatic Arts opened in 1923, and Zoltán Felvinczi Takács, who described Hopp in 1914, became its first director. Objects were transferred from the Museum of Applied Arts, the Museum of Fine Arts, the Ethnographic Museum and the Hungarian National Museum, and private collections such as Vince Wartha's, Jenő Zichy's North Asian material and Imre Schwaiger's Indian collection were added. After 1945 the museum received state gifts from Vietnam, China and North Korea. Hungarian Wikipedia gives about 23,000 objects in 2006, and a 2021 article gives about 30,000. The villa garden still holds the statues, pagodas and memorial columns that Hopp put there.
